data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The smallest positive integer is 18, obtained via an upper-modulus substitution: since x \u2261 4 mod 7 has candidate values 4, 11, 18, ..., we intersect with x \u2261 3 mod 5 by checking only those candidates \u2265 3 (the first remainder), immediately yielding 18 on the third step.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a candidate less than 18 (i.e., 4 or 11) satisfies x \u2261 3 mod 5, minimality fails","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the upper modulus is not 7 (e.g., if 5 is treated as upper), the enumeration starts at 3 and gives 3, 8, 13, 18, hitting 18 on the fourth step instead \u2014 same answer, different path","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If negative candidates were allowed, -17 would also work, but positive minimality restricts to 18","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Enumerate the upper-modulus residue class x \u2261 4 mod 7: candidates are 4, 11, 18, 25, 32, .... Filter by the constraint x \u2261 3 mod 5: 4 mod 5 = 4 (fail), 11 mod 5 = 1 (fail), 18 mod 5 = 3 (pass). Since we enumerate in increasing order and stop at the first hit, 18 is minimal positive.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
